title: From the Seine to the Rhine: the Vintner of Troyes and the Margin of the Book
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Troyes, the winemaker's only son
stops.date_confidence: year 1040 is scholarly consensus; the day 22 February is a later traditional calendrical reconstruction
stops.campa: In a Champagne market town of vineyards and cloth fairs, a son is born to Yitzhak the winemaker and to his wife, sister of the liturgical poet Simon ben Isaac. He is their only child. They name him Shlomo. Troyes has no academy, no famous rabbi, nothing that marks it as the place where the Talmud will be explained to every generation that comes after; it has presses, casks, a small Jewish quarter near the road to Montier-la-Celle, and counts who keep their Jews under protection. The world will know him by four letters: Rashi.
suggested_refs: The vineyards and cloth fairs of eleventh-century Champagne, the economy of Rashi's Troyes

stops.name: Troyes, the jewel cast into the sea
stops.date_confidence: legend; undatable, and no medieval source records it
stops.campa: The story told of his father runs this way. Yitzhak the winemaker comes into possession of a precious stone, and men who are not Jews offer him a great price for it, meaning to set it in the eye of an idol. He carries it aboard ship, and somewhere on open water he lets it fall into the sea rather than sell it. A voice out of heaven answers the loss with a promise: he will father a son who will enlighten the eyes of Israel. No document from the age records any of this. Every generation that copies the commentary copies the story with it.
suggested_refs: The jewel legend of Yitzhak the winemaker, as retold in later hagiographic collections
sources: later folk retellings; absent from primary medieval sources

stops.name: Worms, the wall that opened for his mother
stops.date_confidence: legend; the setting contradicts the attested birthplace of Troyes
stops.campa: A companion legend moves the mother into the story and moves the story into Worms. She is carrying him and walking a narrow lane when two carts come at her from both ends with no room to pass. She presses herself against the stone and the wall opens, taking her body into itself until the carts have gone by. The lane is shown to visitors for centuries, and the stone is pointed out at the exact spot. Troyes, not Worms, is where his mother bore him. The tale has moved his birth downriver to the city that will teach him twenty-five years later, and Worms keeps the lane.
suggested_refs: The Worms lane pointed out to pilgrims as the site of the opened wall

stops.name: Troyes, the first letters on Shavuot
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the festival detail belongs to the custom of Ashkenaz rather than to any record of this child
stops.campa: His father brings him to begin Torah on Shavuot, the feast that commemorates the giving of the Law at Sinai; the boy starts the Book on the anniversary of the day the Book was given. Nothing survives of the schooling that follows. No teacher is named, no first text recorded. What survives is the shape of the practice in a Rhineland-facing town: the alphabet before speech is fluent, verses committed whole and early, and the arguments of the last thousand years learned in the house as though they were talk across a table.
suggested_refs: The Ashkenazi custom of beginning a child's Torah study on Shavuot

stops.name: Troyes, the trades learned beside the text
stops.date_confidence: 1050s, from a late biographical tradition rather than a document
stops.campa: He is trained in what a merchant town requires a man to know: the standards of the coinage, the keeping of loans and accounts, the soldering of metal, the setting of a loom. It shows afterward on every page he writes. When the Talmud argues over a vat, a beam, a knot, a bolt of cloth, he explains it the way a man explains a tool he has held, and where Hebrew fails him he writes the word out in the French of Champagne in Hebrew letters, so the reader will know exactly which object is meant.
suggested_refs: The laaz glosses: Old French vocabulary written in Hebrew characters throughout Rashi's commentaries

stops.name: Troyes, the marriage at seventeen
stops.date_confidence: c.1057; the age is traditional and the wife's name is not preserved in any source
stops.campa: At about seventeen he marries. No source keeps his wife's name, though she is the reason for a pattern the records do keep: for the next dozen years he will cross back from the Rhine to Champagne three times a year, for the Days of Awe, for Passover, for Shavuot, and then return east to the academy. Three daughters will come of this marriage and every heir he has will come through them. He has no son. The house in Troyes is hers to hold through the years he is away at the Rhine.
suggested_refs: The thrice-yearly festival return from the Rhineland, the fullest documented pattern of Rashi's travel

stops.name: Mainz, the yeshiva of Yaakov ben Yakar
stops.date_confidence: c.1057; Encyclopaedia Judaica and the French tradition place this teacher at Mainz, English Wikipedia at Worms, and the contradiction is left standing
stops.campa: He goes east to the Rhine and sits before Yaakov ben Yakar, a pupil of Rabbeinu Gershom. Mainz is a city of stone and river traffic where the Talmud has been read without a break for three generations; Gershom, called the Light of the Exile, is some decades dead and his rulings govern Ashkenaz. The boy out of the vineyard town learns the tractates in the order this house teaches them, and learns the manner of the house as well: the beginner's question answered before the scholar's, the plain sense of the line settled before anything is built on top of it.
suggested_refs: The Mainz academy of Rabbeinu Gershom's successors, where Rashi spent roughly seven years

stops.name: Mainz, the sand where the teachers lie
stops.date_confidence: placed in his Mainz years, c.1058; the earliest surviving stone on the ground is dated 1049, and Rashi's own visits are undocumented
stops.campa: On the sandy slope outside the walls lies the burial ground the community calls the Judensand, the oldest Jewish cemetery in Europe, its earliest surviving stone cut in 1049 while he is still a child in Champagne. A memorial stone for Gershom stands here. His own teacher will be laid here within a few years, in ground he can walk out to from the academy. The vintner's son has crossed a kingdom to sit in front of these men. He will not be buried on this hill. What is taught on it goes west with him instead.
suggested_refs: The Judensand of Mainz, inscribed by UNESCO with the ShUM sites in 2021

stops.name: Mainz, the teacher dies and the tractates go on
stops.date_confidence: the 1064 death of Yaakov ben Yakar is attested; sources disagree on which city Rashi was in when it happened
stops.campa: Yaakov ben Yakar dies in 1064 and is buried on the sand. Rashi does not go home. He stays where he is and passes to Isaac ben Judah, who takes the academy after him, and works the same tractates under a second master. He is about twenty-four and has been seven years away from his wife, seeing her three times a year. Some accounts reverse his Rhineland cities and have him arriving at Mainz only now. The names of the teachers are firm in every version. The map is not, and no version of it can be made to fit the others.
suggested_refs: The grave of Jacob ben Yakar (990-1064) in the Mainz Judensand

stops.name: Worms, the last academy
stops.date_confidence: c.1065-1070; the duration is given as three to five years and is not fixed by any document
stops.campa: The last stage of his education is Worms, under Isaac ben Eliezer HaLevi, chief rabbi of the city. Worms lies a short ride down the Rhine from Mainz and is its rival, with its own academy, its own customs, its own memory of Gershom. Here he finishes, in five years at most and perhaps three. Three men in two cities have now taught him everything he will spend the next forty years setting down, and he sets it down for readers who will never sit in a room with any of them.
suggested_refs: The Worms yeshiva of Isaac ben Eliezer HaLevi, final station of Rashi's Rhineland education

stops.name: Worms, the synagogue of 1034
stops.date_confidence: placed at his arrival in Worms, c.1065; the 1034 founding is attested, and the building he entered no longer exists in any part
stops.campa: The synagogue he studies in is thirty years old when he enters it, built in 1034, the first of its kind in the German lands. Nothing he touched there survives. Crusaders destroy the building in 1096, it is raised again in 1175, burned once more in the pogroms of 1938, and what stands on the site now was reconstructed in 1961. A study room beside it carries his name, the Raschi-Kapelle, though the chapel is later work whose date is not fixed here. The name has outlasted every stone the name was ever attached to.
suggested_refs: The Worms Synagogue and the adjoining Raschi-Kapelle, rebuilt 1961 on the medieval footprint

stops.name: Worms, the stone called Rashi's chair
stops.date_confidence: the identification is local heritage tradition; no medieval source attests the object or the claim
stops.campa: Inside the synagogue a stone seat is set into the wall, and the town shows it as Rashi's chair, the place where he sat to study. No source from his century mentions the seat or the claim. The chair belongs with the jewel and the opened wall: scenery added afterward by people who wanted somewhere to stand and point. He did sit somewhere in this room, for years, at an age when a man is still being made. Which stone it was, nobody wrote down, and so the town chose one and visitors have been sitting in it ever since.
suggested_refs: The stone seat in the Worms synagogue shown as Rashi's chair
sources: Local Worms Jewish-heritage tradition; not corroborated in Encyclopaedia Judaica or academic biographies

stops.name: Lorraine, the road from the Rhine to the Seine
stops.date_confidence: placed at the last crossing, c.1070; the circuit itself runs c.1057-1070, and the coordinates mark an approximate midpoint of the route, not a landmark
stops.campa: Three times a year for a dozen years he makes the crossing, west from the Rhine through Lorraine and the forests to the Seine and Champagne, then east again once the festival has passed. It is some two hundred and fifty miles each way, walked or ridden through country that will be dangerous within a generation and is merely slow now. This is the whole extent of his travel. He never sees Rome or Spain, and he never sets foot in the land his commentary describes verse by verse. From the Seine to the Rhine is the entire geography of the man.
suggested_refs: The Champagne-to-Rhineland road, the only route Rashi is documented to have traveled

segments.name: The Court and the School at Troyes

stops.name: Troyes, the return at twenty-five
stops.date_confidence: c.1065 per Jewish Virtual Library; French Wikipedia says only 'before the age of thirty'
stops.campa: He comes home for good at about twenty-five, and the Rhineland is finished for him except as a place he will one day grieve for. Troyes has no academy. It has his wife, his father's vines, and a small community that has been sending its questions east for answers. He begins answering them himself. Within a few years the traffic reverses direction: questions that used to travel to Mainz and Worms start arriving in Champagne instead, and the replies go out from a winemaker's house in a provincial street.
suggested_refs: Rashi's responsa, the earliest surviving evidence of his authority in Champagne

stops.name: Troyes, the court of Zerach ben Abraham
stops.date_confidence: membership under Zerach is inferred; only the later succession to the court's leadership is attested
stops.campa: He takes a seat on the beth din of Troyes, the court that rules on what may be eaten, whose ox gored whose, whether the wine may be drunk, whether the widow may remarry. Zerach ben Abraham heads it. The work pays nothing; a rabbinate is not yet a salaried office anywhere in Ashkenaz, and men who sit in judgment on one day press grapes on the next. What survives of these years is a body of responsa in which a scholar is visibly learning how much of the Law an ordinary reader can be expected to carry unaided.
suggested_refs: The beth din of Troyes, the court Rashi joined and later led

stops.name: Troyes, the head of the court
stops.date_confidence: late 1060s to 1070s; the year of Zerach ben Abraham's death is not recorded
stops.campa: Zerach dies and Rashi takes the head of the court. He is now the authority for Champagne, and beyond Champagne: letters come from communities with nobody else to ask. He answers in a Hebrew stripped of ornament, without the rhetorical apparatus other authorities use, and he gives the reason together with the ruling. A community that has the reasoning can settle the next case of its kind without writing to Troyes at all. The same habit will govern the commentaries: he is teaching people to work without him, from the first letter he sends.
suggested_refs: The surviving responsa of Rashi, addressed to communities across northern France and the Rhineland

stops.name: Troyes, the yeshiva founded
stops.date_confidence: c.1070; the founding is not dated by any document
stops.campa: He opens a school in Troyes and students come to it from across northern France and from the Rhineland itself, out of the cities that trained him. Within a generation Champagne is what Mainz and Worms had been, and a county whose fame was fairs and cloth is a place men travel to for the Talmud. His sons-in-law come out of this room. So does the method his grandsons will carry into the next century, and they will argue with him on the same page where his words are printed.
suggested_refs: The yeshiva of Troyes, rival to the Rhineland academies within Rashi's own lifetime

stops.name: Troyes, the quarter called la Brosse aux Juifs
stops.date_confidence: the quarter is documented for the eleventh and twelfth centuries; the coordinates estimate the district, and the sources give street names rather than a survey
stops.campa: The Jewish quarter of Troyes sits where the rue Boucherat meets the road to Montier-la-Celle, a district the town will later call la Brosse aux Juifs. A cemetery lies close by, on ground the town now uses for its library. Somewhere within these few streets is the room where the commentary on the Talmud was written, and no deed, no charter, no rent roll names the house. The quarter is documented and the address is lost, which is the ordinary condition of a medieval Jewish street in a French town.
suggested_refs: La Brosse aux Juifs: the junction of rue Boucherat and rue de Montier-la-Celle, medieval Jewish Troyes

stops.name: Troyes, the vines and the harvest
stops.date_confidence: the vintner tradition is not stated outright in any document; the supporting textual evidence in his own writings is attested
stops.campa: He keeps the family vineyards and works them. No document states it plainly. The evidence is in his own handwriting: responsa that apologize for a short answer because the grapes are coming in, and commentaries that describe the vat, the press, the lees, the sealing of a cask with the exactness of a man who did it that same season. The wine of Champagne pays for the school. When he explains a passage on the treading of grapes, the work he is describing is work he came in from that autumn, and the vocabulary is the vocabulary of the yard outside.
suggested_refs: Rashi's harvest-season responsa and his technical wine vocabulary

stops.name: Troyes, under the counts of Champagne
stops.date_confidence: the comital protection is attested in general terms; no charter of privilege from Rashi's own lifetime is cited here
stops.campa: The counts of Champagne hold Troyes, and their fairs are the engine of the county: cloth out of Flanders, spice out of Italy, credit changing hands under comital safeguard. That protection covers the Jews of the town, and it is the reason Troyes has the history the Rhineland cities do not have. When the Rhine burns, Champagne will not. He will spend his last decade writing laments for communities two hundred and fifty miles east while his own street stands untouched, and knowing precisely why it stands.
suggested_refs: The comital protection of the Jews of Troyes under the counts of Champagne

stops.name: Troyes, the first word of the commentary
stops.date_confidence: the Torah commentary is composed across c.1070-1105; individual comments cannot be dated
stops.campa: He begins at the beginning, and the first thing he does is ask why the Book begins where it does: why open with the making of the world rather than with the first commandment given to Israel? He answers in the name of Rabbi Isaac, and the answer turns out to be about title to land. What follows runs the length of the Hebrew Bible, verse by verse, in short sentences, choosing among a thousand years of rabbinic argument and saying each time which reading the words themselves will actually bear.
stops.quote: All the earth belongs to the Holy One, blessed be He; He created it and gave it to whom He pleased.
stops.quote_source: Rashi on Genesis 1:1, trans. M. Rosenbaum and A. M. Silbermann (London, 1929-1934), via Sefaria.org
suggested_refs: The opening comment of Rashi on Genesis 1:1, quoting Rabbi Isaac

stops.name: Troyes, several explanations and one plain sense
stops.date_confidence: the introduction to the Song of Songs is undated within the working life
stops.campa: He states his rule in the preface to the Song of Songs: a verse carries several explanations, and a verse never departs from its plain sense. He is not choosing between the homily and the grammar. He is putting them in order, letting the midrash stand where it illuminates while the literal reading holds the ground underneath it. The rule travels wherever the commentary is copied, and it is a rule that can be turned on the man who wrote it. His own grandson will do exactly that, in print, on the same page.
stops.quote: From one verse, emerge several explanations. [However] in conclusion, a verse does not depart from its literal sense and meaning.
stops.quote_source: Rashi's introduction to the Song of Songs (Rashi on Song of Songs 1:1:1), Sefaria Community Translation, via Sefaria.org
suggested_refs: Rashi's prologue to the Song of Songs, his fullest statement of interpretive method
sources: Sefaria.org, Rashi on Song of Songs 1:1:1

stops.name: Troyes, the dotted word
stops.date_confidence: undated within the composition of the Torah commentary
stops.campa: Esau runs to meet Jacob and kisses him, and the scribes have set dots above the word. Rashi records what the dots are held to mean and refuses to decide: some explain that he did not kiss with his whole heart, while Rabbi Simeon ben Yohai says it is well known that Esau hated Jacob, and that at this moment his pity was truly stirred and he kissed him with his whole heart. Two readings of the same four letters, left standing together on the page. He leaves pairs like this open all through the commentary, and later readers take up whichever side they want and argue from there.
stops.quote: His pity was aroused when he saw him prostrating himself so many times
stops.quote_source: Rashi on Genesis 33:4, trans. Rosenbaum and Silbermann (1929-1934), via Sefaria.org, citing Genesis Rabbah 78:8
suggested_refs: The dotted word vayishakehu at Genesis 33:4 and the dispute recorded in Sifrei Bamidbar 69.2

stops.name: Troyes, the death of Moses written in tears
stops.date_confidence: undated within the composition of the Torah commentary
stops.campa: At the last verses of the Torah he meets the question that cannot be walked around: Moses writes the Book, and the Book records the death of Moses. Is it possible, he asks, that Moses died and then wrote that Moses died there? He sets down both answers the tradition holds. That Moses wrote to this point and Joshua wrote from here on. That the Holy One dictated the closing verses and Moses set them down weeping. He does not rank them. The reader is handed the problem and both solutions and left holding all three.
stops.quote: The Holy One, blessed be He, dictated this, and Moses wrote it in tears.
stops.quote_source: Rashi on Deuteronomy 34:5, trans. Rosenbaum and Silbermann (1929-1934), via Sefaria.org
suggested_refs: Rashi on Deuteronomy 34:5, on the authorship of the Torah's final verses

stops.name: Troyes, the gloss on the whole Talmud
stops.date_confidence: composed across the Troyes decades and still unfinished at his death
stops.campa: The other work is larger: a running gloss on nearly the whole Babylonian Talmud, a text in two languages, compiled over three centuries, unpunctuated, and merciless to a reader who arrives alone. He supplies what the page assumes. Who is speaking, where the objection begins, which word is Aramaic, what the vessel looks like. It is written so that a man in a town with no teacher can open the Talmud and stay inside it. When rabbis later protest that Maimonides's code will let a reader consult a ruling and never open the Talmud at all, they are protesting in the name of this.
suggested_refs: Rashi's Talmud commentary, printed in the inner margin of the standard page
sources: maimonides.journey.json, on the Mishneh Torah controversy

stops.name: Speyer, where the year begins
stops.date_confidence: attested; the killings are attributed chiefly to Count Emicho's contingent rather than to Peter the Hermit's band
stops.campa: On the third of May armed bands moving down the Rhine fall on the Jews of Speyer and kill twelve before the bishop shelters the rest. Rashi never studied here and is not recorded as having entered the city; Speyer is the third of the three Rhine communities, ShUM, and it is where the year opens. From Speyer the bands move to Worms and from Worms to Mainz, along the same river road he rode home on three times a year for a dozen years. News runs ahead of them faster than they march, and does no good at all.
suggested_refs: Speyer, 3 May 1096, first of the Rhineland massacres

stops.name: Worms, the eighteenth of May
stops.date_confidence: attested; the death toll of at least eight hundred is the figure carried by the standard account
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of May the crusading contingent breaks into Worms and at least eight hundred Jews are killed, in the quarter first and then in the bishop's palace where the survivors had been given refuge. Among the dead are the three sons of Isaac ben Eliezer HaLevi, the man who finished Rashi's education in this city. The synagogue of 1034 is destroyed. He is in Troyes, two hundred and fifty miles west, under the safeguard of the counts of Champagne, and learns what happened from people walking west out of it.
suggested_refs: Worms, 18 May 1096: the quarter and the bishop's palace

stops.name: Mainz, the twenty-seventh of May
stops.date_confidence: attested; at least eleven hundred killed, per the standard account of the Rhineland massacres
stops.campa: Nine days later the bands reach Mainz, where the archbishop has taken the community into his own palace, and at least eleven hundred are killed there. The academy where he sat for seven years ends. The Judensand takes what can be buried, and the memorial stone for Gershom stands over a cemetery that is suddenly a great deal larger. In Troyes the news arrives across the summer in pieces, carried by refugees, and it reaches a man who knows the names of the streets they are describing.
suggested_refs: Mainz, 27 May 1096, largest of the Rhineland massacres

stops.name: Troyes, the penitential poems
stops.date_confidence: composed after the massacres of spring 1096; no month is recorded
stops.campa: The selichot are the only thing he writes that is not commentary. They are made to be said aloud on the fast days by congregations that have lost their members, and they enter the liturgy of the Rhine communities that survive the year. He has lost his teachers' families, fellow students, the rooms in which he was made, and both academies. Then he goes back to the tractates, and the commentary continues in the same hand and at the same pace, as though nothing had happened to the man holding the pen.
suggested_refs: Rashi's selichot for the martyrs of 1096, preserved in the Ashkenazi penitential liturgy

segments.name: Daughters, Grandsons, and the Broken Line

stops.name: Ramerupt, the house of Yocheved and Meir
stops.date_confidence: c.1078; the marriage year is traditional and undocumented
stops.campa: His eldest daughter Yocheved marries his student Meir ben Samuel, and the couple settle at Ramerupt, a village some twenty miles north of Troyes. Meir studied in the Troyes school before he married into it. Three sons will be born to them and the tradition will keep all three names, and all three will teach. Rashi has no son of his own. What he has is a daughter, a student he trained himself, and a house on the Aube plain within a day's ride. His method leaves Troyes by that road and by no other.
suggested_refs: Ramerupt in the Aube, seat of Meir ben Samuel and the three Tosafist brothers

stops.name: Troyes, Miriam and Rachel married
stops.date_confidence: c.1080 and the 1080s; neither marriage is dated by a document
stops.campa: The second daughter, Miriam, marries Judah ben Nathan, another of his students, a man who writes early tosafot and who will take up the pen when his father-in-law's hand stops in the middle of a tractate. The third, Rachel, called Belle Assez, a French name in a French town, marries Eliezer ben Shemiah, and that marriage ends in divorce, which the record states plainly and without explanation. What is known of the women of this house is what the genealogies of the men needed to keep.
suggested_refs: The three daughters of Rashi and the students they married

stops.name: Ramerupt, the birth of Rashbam
stops.date_confidence: c.1085 per the dedicated account, which places the birth 'in the vicinity of Troyes'; a family list in another source gives 1080 at Ramerupt
stops.campa: Samuel ben Meir is born, the eldest of the three brothers, called Rashbam. He will study with his grandfather, and then he will write a commentary on the Torah that presses the plain sense harder than his grandfather pressed it, contradicting him in places, by name, in the open. The two readings end up printed within a few inches of each other. The grandfather teaches the boy how to weigh what a verse will actually bear, and the boy weighs it and says so when the answer comes out against him.
suggested_refs: Rashbam's Torah commentary, the plain-sense correction of his grandfather's

stops.name: Ramerupt, the birth of Rabbeinu Tam
stops.date_confidence: c.1100, confirmed; the middle brother Isaac ben Meir is dated 1090 on the strength of a single family list
stops.campa: Jacob ben Meir is born at Ramerupt, youngest of the three brothers, and will be known as Rabbeinu Tam. He is five years old when his grandfather dies. He becomes the dominant figure of the Tosafists, the school that takes Rashi's commentary as the ground to stand on and then argues with nearly every line of it. The argument will be printed on the outer margin of the page his grandfather holds on the inner one. The standard Talmud page is, in its arrangement, a family document.
suggested_refs: The Tosafist school of Rabbeinu Tam, printed on the outer margin of the Talmud page

stops.name: Troyes, the word tahor
stops.date_confidence: the break at Makkot 19b is attested; the tradition that he died in the middle of the word is later embellishment
stops.campa: The commentary breaks off in tractate Makkot at folio 19b. Tradition holds that he died writing the word tahor, pure, and that his son-in-law took the pen from there to the end of the tractate. What is documented is only the break: the gloss stops at 19b and another hand continues. The tradition puts the last stroke on a particular word, which is a way of saying that the man died at work, and everyone who repeats it can name the folio it happened on.
suggested_refs: Makkot 19b, where Rashi's Talmud commentary breaks off and Judah ben Nathan's begins

stops.name: Troyes, the twenty-ninth of Tammuz
stops.date_confidence: attested: 29 Tammuz 4865, corresponding to 13 July 1105
stops.campa: He dies on the twenty-ninth of Tammuz, the thirteenth of July, at about sixty-five. He has never held a paid office, never traveled past the Rhine, never written a book that stands on its own instead of beside another book. He leaves a commentary on the whole Hebrew Bible, a gloss on nearly the whole Talmud, several hundred responsa, penitential poems for the dead of 1096, three daughters, and a school in Champagne that will run for another hundred years on the momentum he gave it.
suggested_refs: 29 Tammuz 4865, the traditional yahrzeit of Rashi

stops.name: Troyes, the burial and the argument about it
stops.date_confidence: burial at Troyes in 1105 is attested; the sources contradict each other on what became of the site and the contradiction is not resolved here
stops.campa: He is buried in the Jewish cemetery of Troyes. What became of the grave afterward is told two ways and the sources do not agree. One account has the site lost and then recovered, with a monument raised over it. Another states plainly that nobody knows where he lies. Both are in print, in reference works of equal standing, and neither gives way. The cemetery itself drops out of the town's records, and the ground goes on being used for other purposes by people who are not told what is under it.
suggested_refs: The lost medieval Jewish cemetery of Troyes

stops.name: Troyes, the son-in-law finishes the tractate
stops.date_confidence: after 1105; the completion is undated
stops.campa: Judah ben Nathan completes the commentary on Makkot from 19b to the end. Other hands close other tractates left open. The work is then transmitted by copying, and the copies are corrected against one another for nearly four centuries before anyone sets it in type; students amend their masters' texts in the margins and the amendments travel on with the manuscript. By the time the thing reaches a press, several hundred hands have been over it, and no copy anywhere is quite the copy he left.
suggested_refs: Judah ben Nathan's continuation of Rashi on Makkot, 19b to the end

stops.name: Reggio di Calabria, the first dated Hebrew book
stops.date_confidence: attested; undated Hebrew incunabula are earlier, so the claim is first dated rather than first printed
stops.campa: Abraham ben Garton sets Rashi's commentary on the Torah in type at Reggio di Calabria and finishes on the eighteenth of February 1475. It is the first printed Hebrew book carrying a date. He prints the commentary alone, without the biblical text it comments on, which says exactly what the commentary had become in three hundred and seventy years: not an accessory to the Book but a book that people would buy by itself. Undated Hebrew printing exists before this. Nothing earlier is dated.
suggested_refs: The 1475 Reggio di Calabria editio princeps of Rashi on the Torah, printed by Abraham ben Garton

stops.name: Reggio di Calabria, the letters that took his name
stops.date_confidence: the typeface derives from fifteenth-century Sephardic semi-cursive handwriting; Rashi himself never wrote in it
stops.campa: To keep commentary visibly distinct from scripture, Garton cuts his type from a Sephardic semi-cursive hand, and the Soncino family and Daniel Bomberg take up the same practice. The letters become the standard face for rabbinic commentary everywhere, and because his is the commentary everyone reads in them they are called Rashi script. He wrote nothing of the kind. He died three and a half centuries before the hand existed and longer before it was cut in metal, and it carries his name regardless.
suggested_refs: Rashi script, the semi-cursive typeface adopted by Garton, the Soncinos, and Bomberg

stops.name: Troyes, the margin the Book is read in
stops.date_confidence: the layout was established by the Soncino tractates of the 1480s and fixed by Bomberg's complete edition of 1520-1523; not every modern edition carries it
stops.campa: Open a standard Talmud anywhere in the world and the arrangement is the one Bomberg fixed between 1520 and 1523: the tractate in the middle of the page, Rashi in the inner margin nearest the spine, the Tosafists of his own family on the outer side arguing back at him. Nearly every standard edition since keeps it. Sixty years after his death Benjamin of Tudela passes through Narbonne and Lunel and finds academies whose Talmud runs on the glosses that came out of Champagne. A vintner's son wrote the margin the Book is now read in.
suggested_refs: The Bomberg Talmud page, 1520-1523, which fixed Rashi's inner-margin position and the foliation still in use
sources: benjamin_de_tudela.journey.json, stops on Narbonne and Lunel

stops.name: Troyes, the globe of Raymond Moretti
stops.date_confidence: twentieth century; the exact year of the monument is not established in the sources reachable here
stops.campa: A professor at the Sorbonne is said to have found an old map showing the medieval cemetery lying beneath an open square in the middle of Troyes. On that ground the Jews of France raise a memorial by the sculptor Raymond Moretti: a great black and white globe with Hebrew letters cut clean through it, so that the letters are openings and the daylight comes through the words. The granite base reads Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, Commentator and Guide. It marks a burial ground. It does not mark a grave.
suggested_refs: Raymond Moretti's pierced globe monument to Rashi in a Troyes public square

stops.name: Troyes, the plaque of 2005
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Yisroel Meir Gabbai, who spends his life finding and marking abandoned Jewish graves across Europe, sets a second plaque at the site. It does not name Rashi. It says: The place you are standing on is the cemetery of the town of Troyes. Nine centuries after the burial, the claim being defended has shrunk to the smallest one available, that this ground is a cemetery, and it has to be cut in stone because the ground itself no longer says so to anyone walking over it.
stops.quote: The place you are standing on is the cemetery of the town of Troyes.
stops.quote_source: Plaque installed by Yisroel Meir Gabbai at the Rashi memorial site, Troyes, 2005
suggested_refs: The 2005 Gabbai plaque at the Troyes memorial square

stops.name: Troyes, the synagogue that carries his name
stops.date_confidence: attested: acquired 1960, prayer hall enlarged 1986, restoration begun 2011, re-inaugurated 4 September 2016
stops.campa: The Synagogue Rachi stands at 5 rue Brunneval, in buildings the community acquired from the diocese in 1960 on the site of an old abbey, a sixteenth-century half-timbered house joined to an eighteenth-century one. The prayer hall is enlarged in 1986, restoration begins in 2011, and the whole is re-inaugurated on the fourth of September 2016 with the Chief Rabbi of France present. Since 1990 a European institute in the town has carried his name into university work. None of it stands on ground he is known to have walked.
suggested_refs: The Synagogue Rachi and the Institut Universitaire Europeen Rachi, Troyes
